The FTC accuses D-Link of manufacturing insecure routers and cameras - PCWorld

This is a fascinating case for me, since I'm a security nut, but really, it seems to me that there are much easier targets than D-Link. I know old 2wire routers (2wire is owned by and is the in house provider for ATT DSL router/modem boxes) came with a universal default administrative password that is difficult to change. Haven't seen a 2wire device in a few years, though, so I can't say how they are now. A few other brands come to mind of course, including Motorola and Asus for just horrendous router security. If the FTC wants to improve IOT security, power to them, but if they are chasing a case where they don't have evidence of a hack occurring, like the case here, they are missing the forest for the trees- yes, security is important, and we should certainly examine companies who put consumers at risk, including those where damage has not yet occurred, but it would make more sense to me to take on these proactive cases after the worst offenders have been dealt with.

I'd love to see more legal initiative for companies to create products that are more secure but I don't know how one could possibly define secure in a court room scenario, everything has vulnerabilities. That said, any move towards better security is a good one.

that's actually quite a good point. How DOES one define secure in a courtroom? Releasing with known security vulnerabilities? Not following industry accepted standards for best practices? It really is a tricky subject. Perhaps a certification not unlike the underwriters laboratories certifications (the UL mark on just about every electronic device that shows that it is safely wired and won't explode when plugging it in) could be mandated that would include basic security principals?

Something like a UL badge is not a bad idea but I see two problems with it. First of all, testing for all of the possible code vulnerabilities in a product takes much more time and energy than just checking whether something will explode or not. Secondly, this would give people a false sense of security, leading them to think that a product is secure just because it has a given badge on it. Basically, you should always be very cautious when somebody claims something is secure.

I don't think a product is well made because it has a UL sticker, though, I just accept that, hey, its not so poorly miswired that it will electrocute me when I plug it in. Finding code vulnerabilities is, yes, difficult, but what about composing a standard of industry best practices, things like "No default password should be universal," and "Passwords will be forced to be changed on first use," Those two things there would make a sizable minority of the IOT products on the market more secure by leaps and bounds, and would be quite easy to test.

"I don't think a product is well made because it has a UL sticker, though, I just accept that, hey, its not so poorly miswired that it will electrocute me when I plug it in." That only applies to people who are actually educated on the matter though. I think the uneducated public would quickly assume something is completely secure if it has a badge warranting a certain level of security on it, even if it just covers basic things.

If we were to have a badge like that though, I think a few requirements would have to be met regarding passwords like you said, but also encryption and at least a certain level of pentesting.
